newsitem.title: USA: Calif. told to repay $1.36 bln to CalPERS - state.
newsitem.headline: Calif. told to repay $1.36 bln to CalPERS - state.

text.p: California has to repay California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS) $1.36 billion for funds the state used to balance its budgets in the early 1990s, state officials said Thursday.

Gov. Pete Wilson's administration had asked the California Supreme Court to review a state appeals court decision issued in February. The 3rd District Court of Appeal ruled that the state improperly withheld the funds from CalPERS.
But the state's Supreme Court refused to rehear the case. As a result, the state has to repay CalPERS the withheld funds, estimated at $1.36 billion, state officials said.
"This is the end of the legal process," said Chris Waddell, chief counsel for the state's Department of Finance. He declined to comment on how the state would repay CalPERS.
The $1.36 billion owed to the pension fund represents nearly three percent of the state's proposed general fund budget for the fiscal year that will begin on July 1.
State lawmakers are expected to consider ways to repay the money during their budget deliberations.
In its ruling, the appeals court affirmed the 1995 decision of a trial court, which had determined that two laws delaying state contributions to CalPERS were unconstitutional.

In September 1992, the state legislature responded to mounting budget pressure by enacting as urgency legislation Senate Bill 1107, which called for the state's employer contributions for general fund employees to be made "semiannually, six months in arrears."
In June 1993, Senate Bill 240 was signed into law, providing that employer contributions be made "annually, 12 months in arrears."
As a result of these two measures, employer contributions that would have been paid during fiscal years 1992-1993 and 1993-1994 were not paid during those years.
In 1994, CalPERS sued the governor and other top state officials, arguing that the measures were unconstitutional.

The trial court hearing the case agreed, ruling in 1995 that "in arrears" financing was unconstitutional, and directed the governor to disregard Senate Bills 1107 and 240, and to reimburse the retirement fund.

The governor appealed the trial court judgement to the 3rd District Court of Appeal. It ruled that CalPERS "members have a contractual right to an actuarially sound retirement system and the 'in arrears' pension financing unconstitutionally impaired that contractual right."
The Supreme Court let the appeals court ruling stand.
A CalPERS spokesperson was not immediately available to comment on the decision.

CalPERS is the nation's largest public pension fund, managing assets in excess of $110 billion. The system provides retirement and health benefits to more than one million active and retired public employees and their families.
